newsitem.title: USA: United Muni High Income fund wins top Lipper spot.
newsitem.headline: United Muni High Income fund wins top Lipper spot.

text.p: Though his United Municipal High Income Fund nabbed a number one ranking among general muni debt funds for 1996, portfolio manager John Holliday admits he makes a bad bet occasionally.
"We owned some of the Retama Racetrack (in) San Antonio, which went broke," Holliday said. "It was worked out and we don't own them any more, but that was our disaster of the year."

But at about $3.5 million, the racetrack bonds accounted for less than one percent of the approximately $411 million fund, whose more frequent successes catapulted it to the top of Lipper Analytical Services long-term national fund category in 1996.

The fund, which is part of the United Group of Mutual Funds and managed by Waddell & Reed, was also Lipper's top high-yield fund in 1996, as well as for the past three-year and five-years periods, Holliday said. Officials at Lipper confirmed those rankings.

Large among the fund's successes in 1996 was a Pennsylvania facility called Riddle Village, he said. The so-called "life care" facility consists of independent living quarters, intermediate care and nursing home care for the elderly. Initially unnrated, the bond was pre-refunded, lifting its credit rating to triple-A, Holliday said.

While the fund typically buys no more than one percent of a non-rated bond, if such bonds "prove themselves," Holliday might increase his holdings. Though such life care facilities have construction and occupancy risks, they are good refunding candidates once they fill up after four or five years, he said.
When Holliday saw the Pennsylvania facility fill quickly, he bought more bonds, raising his Riddle Village holdings to about two percent of his portfolio.
"We were able to buy some bonds in the secondary market, and we owned them for I think less than a year, and the whole thing got pre-refunded," he said.
Holliday's portfolio consists of half non-rated securities and half investment grade debt, he said, adding that his biggest challenge continues to be "finding good high-yield paper."
Looking ahead, Holliday said he has had good success in the hospital sector, and will continue to be buyer there, albeit a cautious one.
"You'd think that with all the changes in hospitals that that would be a problem, but it really hasn't been," he said. "So hospitals continue to be an important part of (the portfolio.)"
The portfolio manager said while he has seen few hospitals "blow up," he does avoid some of them.
"I'd say we are more careful about hospitals than anything, but we still own quite a few, I expect to continue to own (them)," he said.
Hospitals account for approximately 15 percent of his portfolio, Holliday said.
Another area that bears watching is utilities, he said, citing deregulation.

"I don't know of any real serious problems right this moment, but it's certainly an area we are watching," Holliday said. Utilities account for slightly more than 10 percent of his portfolio, Holliday said.
The United Municipal High Income Fund is based in Overland Park, Kan., a Kansas City suburb.
